value: 35 Swedish students (23-34 years old, 74% female) traveled to Indian peninsula (n=18) or Central Africa (n=17)
Median travel duration 34 days (range 14-150); fecal specimens collected median 4 days before and 22 days after return
69% (24/35) had travelers' diarrhea during trip; 67% of hospital-based patient work participation
Shotgun metagenomic sequencing detected >300 antibiotic resistance genes
178 different resistance gene types detected; 23 found in all libraries, 35 in ≥90%
Significant fold changes: sulfonamide 2.6-fold, trimethoprim 7.7-fold, beta-lactams 2.6-fold
12/18 students from India acquired ESBL-producing E. coli (CTX-M-15); none from Africa positive
No antibiotic use within 6 months prior to sampling (inclusion criterion)
Proteobacteria abundance increased in 25/35 students after travel

extraction_warnings: Paper reports aggregate cohort data (n=35: 18 to Indian peninsula, 17 to Central Africa) with before/after paired specimens, not individual sample-level data. Schema requests sample_level granularity, but no per-sample identifiers, per-sample metadata, or sample roster are provided in the paper. The output above represents a single prototypical sample entry with cohort-level characteristics; actual sample-level extraction is not feasible from this aggregate reporting.
Subject IDs and sample IDs are not provided in the paper. Accession number PRJEB7369 is study-level, not sample-specific.
Age is reported as range (23–34 years) for the cohort, not per-sample. Biological sex is reported as aggregate: 74% female (26/35), not per-sample.
Antibiotics_current_use: Paper states 'None of the subjects included were allowed to have taken antibiotics within 6 months prior to fecal sampling', interpreted as No for current use.
Disease: No disease or pathological condition is reported as inclusion criterion; participants were healthy students. Disease field left empty.
Country: Participants were Swedish students; samples collected in Sweden before and after travel.

Subcohort: Paper stratifies by travel destination (Indian peninsula vs. Central Africa); granularity is subgroup_level for resistance gene analysis, not sample_level. Conversion to sample_level forced by schema request results in loss of within-subgroup discrimination.
Location: Paper does not specify collection city within Sweden.
Age_unit and age_group are inferred from range 23–34 years, all adult students.
Batch 1 returned granularity='study_level', differs from batch 0 ('sample_level'); kept batch 0.
This paper is a microbiome and antibiotic resistance study of healthy travelers, not an oncology or clinical disease trial. Most schema fields are not applicable.
The schema focuses on cancer treatment response, neonatal/obstetric outcomes, and clinical disease progression metrics that are not relevant to this epidemiological microbiome study.

The only substantive biomarker data extractable are the antibiotic resistance gene measurements and ESBL acquisition results, which have been captured in biomarker_name, biomarker_unit, and biomarker_value fields.
Travel destination (Indian peninsula vs Central Africa) could be considered subgroups, but results were largely similar between destinations; granularity set to study_level per the overall findings.

Field 'tumor_size_residual_measurement' is not applicable to this microbiome/infectious disease study and has been marked as not_reported.

DNA extraction kit details not provided in accessible text; supplemental methods referenced but not included.
